marseille-vieux-port.d: The Quai des Belges as the fishermen pack up, masts chiming in the breeze, and up above, the Bonne Mère keeping an eye on it all. The Vieux-Port is where every stroll around Marseille begins. And very often where it ends.
marseille-vieux-port.a: The historic heart of Marseille since Greek settlers from Phocaea founded Massalia more than 2,600 years ago, the Vieux-Port (Old Port) is still where the whole city meets: the fish market on the Quai des Belges, the little ferry boat, Norman Foster’s mirrored canopy and sunsets over Fort Saint-Jean. A tile of the Vieux-Port is the ultimate Marseille keepsake.

marseille-notre-dame-de-la-garde.d: You look for her on the way back from holiday, coming out of the tunnel, from the plane window. When you see her, you are home. The Bonne Mère, drawn with her hill and the rooftops below.
marseille-notre-dame-de-la-garde.a: Perched on the highest hill in the city, the basilica of Notre-Dame de la Garde, completed in the 19th century, watches over Marseille and its sailors. Locals fondly call her “la Bonne Mère”, the Good Mother. A Notre-Dame de la Garde tile is the perfect gift for a Marseille native living far away, or for anyone who loves the city.

marseille-mucem.d: The lace-like concrete cube, the footbridge suspended over to Fort Saint-Jean, and the sea just below. The Mucem arrived in 2013, yet it feels as if it has always been there.
marseille-mucem.a: Opened in 2013 at the entrance to the Vieux-Port, the Mucem, the Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations, is instantly recognisable by Rudy Ricciotti’s concrete latticework and the footbridge linking it to Fort Saint-Jean. A symbol of contemporary Marseille, drawn on a ceramic tile.

marseille-la-major.d: Green and white striped stone, Byzantine domes: you could never mistake it for anywhere else. La Major stands between the Panier and the Joliette docks, facing the open sea.
marseille-la-major.a: The cathedral of Sainte-Marie-Majeure, known as La Major, towers over the port of La Joliette with its domes and two-tone stonework. Built in the 19th century at the foot of the Panier, it is one of Marseille’s most impressive monuments.

marseille-vallon-des-auffes.d: Under the great bridge of the Corniche: a few pointu boats, fishermen’s huts and two restaurants serving bouillabaisse. The Vallon des Auffes is a fishing village tucked into the middle of the city, a stone’s throw from the Corniche.
marseille-vallon-des-auffes.a: Nestled beneath the bridge of the Corniche Kennedy, the Vallon des Auffes is a tiny fishing harbour with its cabanons and brightly painted pointus. This hidden corner of the 7th arrondissement is one of the most photographed places in Marseille.

marseille-chateau-d-if.d: Ten minutes by shuttle boat from the Vieux-Port, and you step onto the rock Edmond Dantès escaped from. The Château d’If, François I’s fortress turned legend by Dumas.
marseille-chateau-d-if.a: Built in the 16th century under François I on an islet facing Marseille, the Château d’If became famous through Alexandre Dumas’s The Count of Monte Cristo. It is reached by shuttle boat from the Vieux-Port.

marseille-iles-du-frioul.d: Ratonneau, Pomègues, coves of clear water and the city shrinking behind the boat. The Frioul is where Marseille people go for a beach day when they want a little peace.
marseille-iles-du-frioul.a: The Frioul archipelago, with its limestone islands of Ratonneau and Pomègues, offers coves and turquoise water just a short boat ride from the Vieux-Port. An escape out at sea, without leaving Marseille.

marseille-calanque-sormiou.d: An hour’s walk down, calves burning, and then that water. Sormiou, the largest of Marseille’s calanques, with its cabanons and its little beach tucked at the far end.
marseille-calanque-sormiou.a: In the heart of the Calanques National Park, Sormiou is one of the largest calanques in Marseille, with its beach, its fishermen’s huts and white limestone cliffs plunging into turquoise water.

marseille-calanque-morgiou.d: A tiny harbour, fishing boats and cabanons huddled against the rock. Morgiou is Marseille without the city: you forget you are twenty minutes from the centre.
marseille-calanque-morgiou.a: Morgiou shelters a little fishing port and cabanons at the end of a deep, narrow calanque in the Calanques National Park. The end of the world, just a few kilometres from central Marseille.

marseille-palais-longchamp.d: A sweeping semicircular colonnade, a monumental cascade and a museum on either side. The Palais Longchamp was built in the 19th century to celebrate the arrival of water from the Durance in Marseille. No less.
marseille-palais-longchamp.a: Built in the 19th century to celebrate the waters of the Durance reaching Marseille, the Palais Longchamp spreads out its colonnade and monumental fountain, and houses the Fine Arts Museum and the Natural History Museum.

marseille-tour-cma-cgm.d: 147 metres of glass by Zaha Hadid, rising above the Joliette docks. You can see it from everywhere, even from the motorway: the CMA CGM tower has become a landmark of today’s Marseille.
marseille-tour-cma-cgm.a: Designed by the architect Zaha Hadid and opened in 2011, the CMA CGM tower rises 147 metres in the heart of the Euroméditerranée district. Head office of the Marseille shipping company, it has become one of the city’s landmarks, visible from the sea as well as from the hills.

marseille-velodrome.d: The rippling roof, the roar you can hear from the Boulevard Michelet on match nights. Olympique de Marseille fans need no further explanation.
marseille-velodrome.a: Opened in 1937 and transformed for Euro 2016 with its undulating roof, the Stade Vélodrome is the home ground of Olympique de Marseille. With around 67,000 seats, it is one of the largest stadiums in France and a legendary place of Marseille passion.

marseille-panisse.d: Crisp outside, meltingly soft inside, served piping hot in a paper cone on the harbour at L’Estaque. Panisse is Marseille’s afternoon snack par excellence. This one, at least, never goes cold.
marseille-panisse.a: Panisse, a chickpea-flour batter set, sliced into rounds or chips and fried golden, has been eaten hot from a paper cone on the harbour and at L’Estaque for generations. Its name also recalls Panisse, the Vieux-Port sailmaker created by Marcel Pagnol in Marius and Fanny.

marseille-david.d: “Meet you at the David.” Every Marseille local has said it at least once. The marble statue set up in 1903 at the Prado roundabout, facing the beaches.
marseille-david.a: A marble replica of Michelangelo’s David, the statue was installed in 1903 at the end of the Avenue du Prado, facing the beaches. Locals simply call it “le David” and have made it the seafront’s classic meeting point.

marseille-corniche-kennedy.d: The longest bench in the world, so they say, with the sea in front and the Frioul in the distance. People walk it, scoot along it, run it, or sit and watch everyone else go by. The Corniche Kennedy.
marseille-corniche-kennedy.a: Laid out in the 19th century and renamed in honour of President John F. Kennedy, the Corniche runs along the sea from Les Catalans to the Prado. Lined with a stone bench several kilometres long, it passes over the Vallon des Auffes and looks out over the Frioul and the Château d’If.

marseille-le-panier.d: Streets that climb, steps that tumble down, washing at the windows and façades in every colour. The Panier, Marseille’s oldest neighbourhood, where it all began 2,600 years ago.
marseille-le-panier.a: Perched above the Vieux-Port, the Panier is Marseille’s oldest district, standing on the site of the Greek city of Massalia founded around 600 BC. Wander through its colourful lanes, craft workshops and the Vieille Charité, built in the 17th century to plans by Pierre Puget.

marseille-canebiere.d: The name “Canebière” comes from the Provençal word canebe, the hemp used by rope-makers long ago. Today it is the avenue of trams, cafés and victory nights, running straight down to the Vieux-Port.
marseille-canebiere.a: The city’s historic thoroughfare, the Canebière links the Vieux-Port to the Réformés district. Its name comes from the Provençal canebe, hemp, a reminder of the rope-makers who once made ships’ rigging here. Celebrated in countless songs, it remains the symbolic heart of Marseille.

marseille-cite-radieuse.d: A vertical city on stilts, with indoor streets, a hotel and a school on the roof. Le Corbusier designed it in 1952; Marseille people call it “la Maison du Fada”, the madman’s house. A UNESCO World Heritage site.
marseille-cite-radieuse.a: Completed in 1952, the Cité radieuse was the first Unité d’habitation designed by Le Corbusier: a vertical city with flats, shops, a hotel and a roof terrace. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2016, along with other works by the architect.

marseille-fort-saint-jean.d: King René’s tower, Louis XIV’s ramparts and, just across the water, the Pharo. Fort Saint-Jean has guarded the entrance to the Vieux-Port for centuries, and its gardens offer one of the finest views of the city.
marseille-fort-saint-jean.a: Built in the 17th century under Louis XIV around the older tower of King René, Fort Saint-Jean stands guard over the entrance to the Vieux-Port together with Fort Saint-Nicolas. Linked to the Mucem by a footbridge since 2013, it is now home to gardens and exhibitions open to the public.

marseille-le-prado.d: Sand, lawns where you spread out your towel after work, and the sea as far as the eye can see. The Prado beaches: summer, Marseille-style.
marseille-le-prado.a: At the end of the Avenue du Prado, the Prado seaside park stretches along the coast with its beaches, its lawns and the nearby Parc Borély. Created from the late 1970s onwards, it has become Marseille’s great place to unwind, around the statue of David.

cote-bleue-port-niolon.d: You reach it down a winding road. The train passes just above, on its viaduct. Down below: a few boats, some divers, and water of incredible clarity. Niolon.
cote-bleue-port-niolon.a: A small village of Le Rove clinging to the rocks, Niolon is known for its clear water, its seabed loved by divers and the Côte Bleue railway viaduct that runs above the harbour.

cote-bleue-calanque-mejean.d: A handful of cabanons, brightly painted boats and crystal-clear water at the end of a calanque. Méjean is the Côte Bleue just the way we love it: simple and unpretentious.
cote-bleue-calanque-mejean.a: In the commune of Ensuès-la-Redonne, the Calanque de Méjean is a sheltered cove lined with fishermen’s huts, where boats drop anchor for a swim. One of the Côte Bleue’s quiet treasures.

cote-bleue-port-la-redonne.d: A harbour so narrow the boats almost touch. All around, pine woods and silence. La Redonne.
cote-bleue-port-la-redonne.a: The little harbour of La Redonne, in Ensuès-la-Redonne, hides at the end of a calanque spanned by the viaduct of the Côte Bleue railway line. Boats, cabanons and pine woods: absolute calm.

cote-bleue-carry-le-rouet.d: Sea urchin capital every winter, seaside resort in summer. Carry-le-Rouet, with its harbour, its colourful houses and its waterfront promenade, whatever the season.
cote-bleue-carry-le-rouet.a: A seaside resort on the Côte Bleue, Carry-le-Rouet is known for its harbour, its coves and its famous winter sea urchin feasts, the oursinades. A seaside village where many people have summer memories.

cote-bleue-sausset-les-pins.d: The umbrella pines, the corniche where you walk in the evening and the little lighthouse at the end of the harbour. If you spent your summers in Sausset-les-Pins, you will recognise it straight away.
cote-bleue-sausset-les-pins.a: A former fishing village, Sausset-les-Pins charms visitors with its corniche, its small harbour and its umbrella pines right by the water. A Sausset-les-Pins tile is a gift for everyone who grew up or spent their holidays there.

cote-bleue-port-carro.d: The last fishing village before the Gulf of Fos. In Carro, people still buy their fish straight from the quay, and the sea wind never really stops.
cote-bleue-port-carro.a: At the far end of the Côte Bleue, Carro is the fishing port of Martigues, with its fish market and a spot loved by surfers and kitesurfers when the wind picks up.
